# Introduction

## Background

A grocery retail chain sells chips across its stores and records every purchase
made with a loyalty card. Each card is linked to two labels: a life stage
(from young singles and couples through families to retirees) and a customer
tier (Budget, Mainstream or Premium) that reflects purchasing power. Together,
the labels show who is buying what.

Between July 2018 and June 2019, the cleaned data record
`{python} f"{len(df_cust):,}"` chip transactions made by
`{python} f"{df_cust['LYLTY_CARD_NBR'].nunique():,}"` loyalty cards across
`{python} df_cust['STORE_NBR'].nunique()` stores, with total sales of
`{python} f"${df_cust['TOT_SALES'].sum():,.0f}"`.

## The Business Question

Decisions about promotions, pricing and shelf space are easier when it is clear
which customer groups matter and how they behave. A customer group that pays
more per pack may be more willing to buy higher-priced products, and it could
be treated differently from a group that mainly buys at low prices.

This report examines one segment in detail: **Mainstream Young
Singles/Couples**. The question is whether customers in this segment pay a
higher average price per pack than all other customers, and whether the
difference is larger than chance.

## Approach

The data are cleaned and joined, then summarized by customer segment. The
segment's average price per pack is compared with that of all other customers
using a permutation test, which asks whether a gap this large could arise by
chance, and a bootstrap confidence interval, which shows how precisely the gap
is estimated. Each loyalty card contributes one price, so that customers with
many purchases do not dominate the result.


# Data

## Source

The data come from the Quantium retail analytics simulation and consist of two
files: a transaction file, where each row is one product bought in one
transaction between July 2018 and June 2019, and a customer file giving each
loyalty card a life stage and a customer tier. The two files are joined on the
loyalty card number.

The raw transaction file contains `{python} f"{n_cards_raw:,}"` loyalty cards
and `{python} n_stores_raw` stores. Cleaning removes
`{python} f"{n_cards_raw - n_cards:,}"` cards, which bought only salsa or the
removed bulk purchases and therefore have no chip records, and
`{python} n_stores_raw - n_stores` store whose records were all removed.

## Unit of Observation

In the cleaned data, each row is one product bought in one transaction. For the
statistical comparison, the unit is one loyalty card, using the card's total
sales divided by its total packs. This ensures that a customer with many
purchases is not counted many times.

## Variables

| Variable | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `LYLTY_CARD_NBR` | Loyalty card number, used to join the two files |
| `LIFESTAGE` | Life stage of the customer (7 groups), as labeled by the retailer |
| `PREMIUM_CUSTOMER` | Customer tier: Budget, Mainstream or Premium |
| `PROD_QTY`, `TOT_SALES` | Packs bought and dollars spent on a transaction record |
| `price_per_pack` | `TOT_SALES / PROD_QTY`, derived |


## Cleaning

Three problems were found in the raw transaction file and removed
(@tbl-cleaning): one exact duplicate record; salsa products, which are not
chips and so fall outside the question; and two bulk purchases of 200 packs
each, both from a single loyalty card with no other purchases. These are almost
certainly commercial purchases and would distort the averages. The threshold of
more than 10 packs in one record is a judgement call.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-cleaning
#| tbl-cap: "Records removed at each cleaning step."
labels = {
    "raw rows": "Raw transaction records",
    "exact duplicates removed": "Exact duplicates removed",
    "salsa lines removed": "Salsa records removed (not chips)",
    "bulk-purchase lines removed": "Bulk purchases removed (more than 10 packs)",
    "rows kept": "Records kept for analysis",
}
cleaning_log = pd.read_csv("data/processed/cleaning_log.csv", index_col=0).rename(index=labels)
cleaning_log["count"] = cleaning_log["count"].map("{:,}".format)
cleaning_log.rename(columns={"count": "Records"}).rename_axis("Step")
```

## Missing Data

```{python}
#| label: missing-check
#| include: false
n_missing_values = int(df_cust.isna().sum().sum())
all_days = pd.date_range(df_cust["DATE"].min(), df_cust["DATE"].max())
missing_days = all_days.difference(pd.DatetimeIndex(df_cust["DATE"].unique()))
missing_text = ", ".join(d.strftime("%d %B %Y") for d in missing_days)
```

The analysis data contain `{python} n_missing_values` empty cells, so no values
needed to be filled in or removed. The calendar days in the period with no
transactions are: `{python} missing_text`. This is consistent with stores being
closed on Christmas Day, and it is treated as a real-world gap, not a data
error. No imputation was needed.

## Joining the files

```{python}
#| label: join-check
#| include: false
cust = pd.read_csv("data/raw/Q_Purchase_Behaviour.csv")
n_cust_cards = len(cust)
unmatched = int((~df_cust["LYLTY_CARD_NBR"].isin(cust["LYLTY_CARD_NBR"])).sum())
rows_before = int(
    pd.read_csv("data/processed/cleaning_log.csv", index_col=0).loc["rows kept", "count"]
)
rows_after = len(df_cust)

# The report stops with an error if any of these checks fails
assert cust["LYLTY_CARD_NBR"].is_unique
assert unmatched == 0
assert rows_before == rows_after
```

The transaction file records what was bought but not who bought it, and the
customer file records each loyalty card's life stage and tier but has no
prices. The two files were joined on `LYLTY_CARD_NBR`. This is a many-to-one
join: many transaction records can belong to one card, but each card appears
once in the customer file. A left join kept every transaction, and the option
`validate="many_to_one"` makes the join stop with an error if the customer file
ever contained duplicate cards.

Three checks confirm that the join behaved as intended. The customer file lists
`{python} f"{n_cust_cards:,}"` cards, each appearing exactly once. Transactions
without a matching customer: `{python} unmatched`. The number of transaction
records was `{python} f"{rows_before:,}"` before the join and
`{python} f"{rows_after:,}"` after it, so the join neither lost nor duplicated
records.


# Methods

## Outcome and Unit of Analysis

The outcome is the price per pack of chips. For each loyalty card, total sales
were divided by the total number of packs bought, giving one value per card.
Cards, rather than individual transaction records, are the unit of analysis
because records from the same card are not independent of one another: a card
that buys cheap packs once tends to do so again. Treating each record as a
separate observation would overstate how much evidence the data contain.

## Comparison

The focus group consists of cards in the Young Singles/Couples life stage with
the Mainstream tier. The comparison group contains all other cards. The test
statistic is the difference in mean price per pack, focus group minus
comparison group.

## Permutation Test

The null hypothesis states that segment membership has no relationship with
price per pack. If this were true, the segment labels could be reassigned to
cards at random without changing the distribution of the statistic. The
procedure was:

1. Compute the observed difference in means.
2. Shuffle the group labels at random, keeping both group sizes fixed, and
   recompute the difference.
3. Repeat the shuffle `{python} f"{N_PERM:,}"` times. The shuffled differences
   form the null distribution, which shows the gaps that arise by chance alone.
4. The two-sided p-value is the share of shuffled differences whose absolute
   value is at least as large as the observed one. One is added to both the
   numerator and the denominator, so the p-value is never exactly zero. The
   smallest value that this procedure can report is therefore
   `{python} f"{1 / (N_PERM + 1):.4f}"`.

## Bootstrap Interval

To describe the size of the gap, and how precisely it is estimated, a
percentile bootstrap was used. Each group was resampled with replacement to its
original size, and the difference in means was recomputed. This was repeated
`{python} f"{N_BOOT:,}"` times. The 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the
resampled differences form a 95% interval for the gap. The same procedure
applied to a single group gives an interval for that group's mean, which is
used to compare all customer segments in the figures below.

## Reproducibility and Checks

All random operations use a generator created from the fixed seed
`{python} SEED`, so every run of the report gives identical numbers. Three
checks supported the implementation. The functions were first run on artificial
data with a known gap, then repeated under several different seeds to confirm
that the results do not depend on the seed, and finally compared with the
corresponding SciPy routines. Their outcomes are reported with the results.
